(CNN) -- Watch out! Lock up your loved ones! Another bloated, over-produced, high-concept monstrosity has escaped from the labs at Dreamworks Animation, and it's out to devour your kids. Susan, aka "Ginormica," has to save the world in "Monsters vs. Aliens." But don't be too alarmed. "Monsters vs. Aliens" is relatively harmless -- a toothless satire with a knee-jerk feminist theme and a sorry excuse for a plot. That sounds harsh, I know. Who doesn't want to see a 50-foot woman careening through San Francisco on skates that turn out to be automobiles -- the ultimate demolition roller derby? But think about that, just for a second. Roller skates work because they have fixed wheels. Try it with motorcars and you won't get very far. Is that too picky? Perhaps, but you wouldn't find Pixar playing so fast and loose with the laws of physics, and that kind of inattention to detail is typical of the lackadaisical storytelling here and in other Dreamworks animated features. (The talent pool for this one includes the directors of "Shrek 2" and "Shark Tale" and the writers of "Kung Fu Panda" and "The Rocker," incidentally.) High concepts, top-notch voice talent and scattershot pop cultural references are no compensation for a coherent script. The XXXL lady in question -- dubbed "Ginormica" by her U.S. military guards -- starts out plain and petite Susan Murphy (voiced by Reese Witherspoon), until a meteorite hits her just minutes before she's supposed to tie the knot with unctuous chauvinist Derek (Paul Rudd). Her rapid growth spurt saves her from that particular fate worse than death, even if at first glance her new roommates don't look like much of an improvement. There's Dr. Cockroach (Hugh Laurie), a mad scientist who semi-advertently mutated with a bug; B.O.B. (Seth Rogen) an amorphous blue jelly-like blob who gets on just fine without a brain; Missing Link (Will Arnett), a gung-ho amphibian who's all mouth; and a giant dust mite called Insectosaurus who isn't voiced by anyone because he doesn't have anything to say. Sci-fi fans will have fun counting off the references to myriad classics -- "Close Encounters of the Third Kind," "Invaders from Mars," "The Fly," "The Creature from the Black Lagoon," "The Blob," "Mothra" and "Attack of the 50-Foot Woman," for starters -- and noting a few clever bits and pieces (Kiefer Sutherland, as General W.R. Monger, riffs on George C. Scott in "Dr. Strangelove"). The trouble is, once the introductions are over, the filmmakers can only launch their desperately limp plot: The White House turns to these monstrous superheroes to save the planet from evil Gallaxhar (Rainn Wilson), a squidlike creature with four eyes and twice as many legs, and a one-eyed tin robot to do his dirty work for him. Ginormica gets a kick-butt finale, and is a much stronger character -- in any number of ways -- than the movie's president. (In a genuinely witty casting touch he's voiced by Stephen Colbert.) That may be good politics or at least a sound marketing decision from the studio's perspective -- it's been awhile since a family animated feature produced a genuinely strong female character (unless you count "Coraline," which was way too scary for my family) -- but Susan's self-esteem is an awfully long time coming. iReport.com: What do you think of 'Monsters vs. Aliens'? (Bizarrely -- and maybe it's just my imagination -- Gallaxhar bears a passing resemblance to President Obama. I wonder ... would that make Susan/Ginormica a surrogate for Sarah Palin or Hillary Clinton?) Visually, too, "Monsters vs Aliens" is undistinguished, although its shortcomings may be disguised if you seek out the 3-D version. Funny how 3-D movies tend to produce two-dimensional characters, with "Coraline" again the exception to the rule. Jocular and unpretentiously trashy, "Monsters vs. Aliens" should be a lot of fun -- and it is, in places. But the truth is it's as hung up on itself as Susan's preening fiance. Hand on heart, I had a better time at "Space Chimps." "Monsters vs. Aliens" runs 94 minutes and is rated PG. For Entertainment Weekly's take, click here.

(CNN) -- Beware! Shield your loved ones! Another bloated, over-produced, high-concept behemoth has escaped from the laboratories of DreamWorks Animation, poised to devour your children's attention. Susan, otherwise known as "Ginormica," must save the world in "Monsters vs. Aliens." Yet there's little cause for alarm. "Monsters vs. Aliens" proves relatively harmless—a toothless satire built around a reflexive feminist theme and a threadbare excuse for a plot.

I recognize that assessment sounds harsh. After all, who wouldn't relish watching a fifty-foot woman careening through San Francisco on skates that transform into automobiles—the ultimate demolition roller derby? But consider this for a moment: roller skates function because their wheels are fixed. Attempt the same maneuver with actual cars, and you won't get very far. Is this too pedantic a critique? Perhaps—but Pixar would never play so loosely with the laws of physics, and such carelessness with detail typifies the lackadaisical storytelling found here and throughout DreamWorks' animated catalog. (Notably, the talent behind this production includes the directors of "Shrek 2" and "Shark Tale," alongside the writers of "Kung Fu Panda" and "The Rocker.") Ambitious concepts, top-tier voice talent, and scattershot pop-culture references cannot compensate for the absence of a coherent script.

Our XXXL heroine—christened "Ginormica" by her U.S. military guards—begins life as the unassuming Susan Murphy (voiced by Reese Witherspoon), until a meteorite strikes her mere minutes before her wedding to the unctuous, chauvinistic Derek (Paul Rudd). Her sudden growth spurt spares her from that particular fate worse than death, though at first glance, her new companions hardly seem an improvement. Among them: Dr. Cockroach (Hugh Laurie), a mad scientist who inadvertently merged with an insect; B.O.B. (Seth Rogen), an amorphous blue, gelatinous blob who manages perfectly well without a brain; Missing Link (Will Arnett), a gung-ho amphibian who is all bravado; and a colossal dust mite named Insectosaurus, who requires no voice actor since he has nothing to say.

Science-fiction enthusiasts will delight in cataloging the film's homages to numerous classics—"Close Encounters of the Third Kind," "Invaders from Mars," "The Fly," "Creature from the Black Lagoon," "The Blob," "Mothra," and "Attack of the 50-Foot Woman," among others—along with a handful of clever touches, such as Kiefer Sutherland's General W.R. Monger channeling George C. Scott's performance in "Dr. Strangelove." The trouble is that once the introductions conclude, the filmmakers can only limp forward with a desperately thin plot: the White House enlists these monstrous heroes to save the planet from the villainous Gallaxhar (Rainn Wilson), a squid-like creature with four eyes, twice as many legs, and a one-eyed tin robot to execute his dirty work.

Ginormica is granted a rousing final showdown and emerges as a far stronger character—in numerous respects—than the film's president, voiced with genuine wit by Stephen Colbert. This may reflect sound politics, or at least astute marketing on the studio's part—it has, after all, been some time since a family animated feature offered a truly compelling female protagonist (unless one counts "Coraline," which proved far too frightening for my household)—but Susan's journey to self-assurance takes an inordinately long time to unfold.

iReport.com: What do you think of "Monsters vs. Aliens"?

(Curiously—and perhaps this is merely my imagination—Gallaxhar bears a fleeting resemblance to President Obama. One wonders: might this render Susan/Ginormica a stand-in for Sarah Palin or Hillary Clinton?)

Visually, too, "Monsters vs. Aliens" fails to distinguish itself, though its shortcomings may be somewhat obscured in the 3-D presentation. It is curious how 3-D films so often yield two-dimensional characters, with "Coraline" once again standing as the exception. Playful and unabashedly trashy, "Monsters vs. Aliens" ought to be great fun—and in places, it is. Yet the truth remains that the film is as enamored with itself as Susan's preening fiancé. Hand on heart, I found more enjoyment in "Space Chimps."

"Monsters vs. Aliens" runs 94 minutes and is rated PG.

# A Critical Look at "Monsters vs. Aliens": Ambitious Concept, Uneven Execution

DreamWorks Animation's "Monsters vs. Aliens" presents an intriguing premise wrapped in a colorful, action-packed package, though critical reception reveals significant shortcomings beneath its entertaining surface. The film follows Susan Murphy, an ordinary woman whose life takes an extraordinary turn on what should have been the happiest day of her life. Struck by a mysterious meteorite on her wedding day, Susan undergoes a dramatic transformation, growing to an astonishing 50 feet tall. Now dubbed "Ginormica" by the government agents who capture her, she finds herself thrust into a world far removed from her previous ordinary existence.

## A Critique of Substance Over Style

Despite its imaginative high-concept setup, the film has drawn criticism for failing to deliver on its potential. Reviewers have characterized the movie as a "toothless satire," suggesting that while it gestures toward feminist themes—using Susan's transformation as a metaphor for female empowerment and self-discovery—the execution remains superficial rather than substantive. The narrative, critics argue, prioritizes spectacle over meaningful storytelling, resulting in a plot that feels thin and underdeveloped despite the richness of its premise.

## Logical Gaps in the Details

Beyond thematic concerns, the film has faced scrutiny for its internal logical inconsistencies. One frequently cited example involves Ginormica's use of motorized roller skates during action sequences—a detail that doesn't hold up under scrutiny. Critics have pointed out that the skates' fixed-wheel design would make the kind of dynamic, multidirectional movement depicted in the film physically implausible. This seemingly minor detail becomes emblematic of a larger pattern: a willingness to sacrifice internal consistency for the sake of visual excitement.

## A Studio Comparison

This critique extends into a broader commentary on DreamWorks Animation's storytelling approach as a whole. The review draws an unflattering comparison to Pixar, whose films are often celebrated for their meticulous attention to detail and internal narrative logic. Where Pixar films tend to construct their fantastical worlds with careful consideration of cause and effect, "Monsters vs. Aliens" is described as exhibiting a more "lackadaisical" approach—one that prioritizes momentum and spectacle over the kind of rigorous world-building that elevates animated storytelling to its highest form.

## An Ensemble Cast of Memorable Characters

Despite these narrative shortcomings, the film benefits from a colorful ensemble of monster characters who accompany Susan on her journey. She's joined by Dr. Cockroach, a brilliant but unstable scientist who has merged human and insect DNA; B.O.B., a good-natured but simple-minded blob lacking a brain; Missing Link, a half-fish, half-ape creature frozen in time; and Insectosaurus, a colossal, gentle larva-like monster. This eclectic group is brought to life by a talented voice cast, including Hugh Laurie, Seth Rogen, and Will Arnett, whose performances lend personality and charm to characters that might otherwise feel like mere plot devices. Their chemistry and comedic timing provide some of the film's most engaging moments, even as the broader narrative struggles to achieve the depth its premise seems to promise.

# Monsters vs. Aliens: A Missed Opportunity for DreamWorks Animation

"Monsters vs. Aliens," the 2009 animated feature from DreamWorks Animation, presents an ambitious premise that unfortunately fails to deliver on its potential. The film follows Susan Murphy, an ordinary young woman whose life is upended on her wedding day when she is struck by a mysterious meteor and transformed into a fifty-foot giant. Rechristened "Ginormica" by the government, Susan is swept away from her old life and imprisoned in a secret facility alongside a menagerie of other monstrous outcasts—each one a affectionate parody of classic creature-feature icons.

Her fellow captives include B.O.B., a gelatinous, brainless blue blob with an insatiable appetite and childlike innocence; Dr. Cockroach Ph.D., a mad scientist who accidentally mutated himself into a human-cockroach hybrid; The Missing Link, a prehistoric fish-ape hybrid frozen in time; and Insectosaurus, a colossal, gentle grub mutated by nuclear testing. When the alien overlord Gallaxhar arrives on Earth in search of the very meteor that transformed Susan, intent on harvesting its power to build a clone army and conquer the planet, the government has no choice but to unleash this ragtag team of monsters as humanity's only line of defense.

Despite this colorful setup and the novelty of its "monsters as heroes" concept, critical reception of the film has been lukewarm at best. Many reviewers have labeled "Monsters vs. Aliens" a "toothless satire," arguing that it squanders its rich premise of playfully subverting classic monster movie tropes. Rather than delivering sharp, memorable commentary or genuinely inventive humor, the film settles for surface-level gags and predictable plot beats that fail to leave a lasting impression.

Critics have also pointed to a distinct lack of narrative depth, noting that the story feels thin and formulaic, relying heavily on familiar underdog and save-the-world arcs without adding meaningful twists or emotional resonance. Furthermore, inattention to detail in both the writing and pacing has been cited as a recurring issue, with some reviewers suggesting that the film feels rushed or incomplete in its world-building, as though the filmmakers were more concerned with spectacle than substance.

This is particularly notable given the film's considerable star power, with a voice cast including Reese Witherspoon, Seth Rogen, Hugh Laurie, and Will Arnett, among others—talent that critics argue is ultimately wasted on underdeveloped characters and a script that doesn't match their comedic or dramatic capabilities. The film's reliance on 3D visual spectacle and celebrity voice casting, while eye-catching, has been seen by many as compensating for—rather than complementing—weaker storytelling fundamentals.

When placed alongside contemporaries in the animated film landscape, particularly Pixar's offerings during the same era, "Monsters vs. Aliens" suffers by comparison. While Pixar films of the period were consistently praised for their emotional intelligence, layered storytelling, and ability to appeal to both children and adults on multiple levels, "Monsters vs. Aliens" is often viewed as prioritizing high-concept marketing and visual gimmickry over the kind of narrative craftsmanship that elevates animated films into truly memorable cinematic experiences. Ultimately, the film stands as an example of style triumphing over substance—a visually ambitious project that never quite finds the heart or wit needed to make its clever premise truly soar.

# Smart Security: The Rise of CNN-Powered Watch Locks

In the ever-evolving landscape of wearable technology, a fascinating convergence has emerged between artificial intelligence and personal security: the CNN-powered smartwatch lock system. This innovative approach combines Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) with wearable devices to create sophisticated authentication mechanisms that go far beyond traditional passcodes.

## Understanding the Technology

Convolutional Neural Networks, a class of deep learning algorithms particularly effective at processing visual and pattern-based data, have found a unique application in smartwatch security. These networks excel at recognizing subtle patterns—whether in images, gestures, or even physiological signals—making them ideal candidates for enhancing how our watches lock and unlock.

Modern smartwatches equipped with CNN-based authentication can analyze:

- **Wrist gesture patterns**: Unique movement signatures created when a user naturally raises or rotates their wrist
- **Biometric data**: Heart rate patterns, skin conductance, or even micro-vibrations unique to an individual
- **Facial recognition**: For watches with camera capabilities, CNNs can process facial features for quick authentication
- **Behavioral biometrics**: How a person types on a small screen or swipes through notifications

## Why CNNs Excel at This Task

The layered architecture of CNNs allows them to progressively learn increasingly complex features—starting with simple edges or basic sensor readings, then building toward recognizing complete patterns unique to an individual. This makes them remarkably good at distinguishing legitimate users from impostors, even when environmental conditions vary (different lighting, wrist positions, or movement speeds).

## Balancing Security and Convenience

The primary appeal of CNN-powered lock systems lies in their ability to provide seamless security. Rather than requiring users to repeatedly enter PINs, these systems can continuously verify identity in the background, locking the device automatically when it detects the watch has been removed or when biometric signals no longer match the registered user—all while minimizing friction for the legitimate wearer.

## Challenges and Considerations

Despite their promise, these systems face hurdles:

- **Processing power**: CNNs traditionally require significant computational resources, challenging for battery-constrained wearables
- **Privacy concerns**: Continuous biometric monitoring raises questions about data storage and potential misuse
- **False positive/negative rates**: Balancing security (avoiding unauthorized access) with usability (avoiding frustrating lockouts) remains an ongoing challenge

## Looking Forward

As edge computing capabilities improve and CNN architectures become more efficient, we can expect smartwatches to offer increasingly sophisticated, low-power authentication systems. Future iterations may combine multiple CNN-based recognition methods, creating multi-factor authentication that happens invisibly, protecting our most personal wearable devices without ever requiring us to think about it.

The marriage of CNN technology with watch locking mechanisms represents just one example of how deep learning is quietly transforming everyday security—making our devices smarter, safer, and more attuned to who we truly are.

# "Monsters vs. Aliens": When Bigger Isn't Always Better

*By a Critic Who Has Seen Too Many Talking Animals This Year*

DreamWorks Animation's "Monsters vs. Aliens" arrives with the subtlety of an asteroid crashing through your living room—loud, colorful, and leaving you wondering what exactly you just witnessed.

**The Premise, Such As It Is**

Susan Murphy (voiced by Reese Witherspoon) gets zapped by a meteor on her wedding day and grows to 49 feet, 11 inches tall. Naturally, the government's response isn't hospitalization or, say, *concern*—it's immediate imprisonment in a secret facility alongside a motley crew of monsters including a cockroach-headed scientist and a gelatinous blue blob with no discernible rules governing his physics. When aliens invade, this ragtag group becomes Earth's last hope. Because of course they do.

**Let's Talk Plot Holes**

Why does the government have a secret monster prison just *sitting there* fully staffed and ready, as if they were expecting exactly this scenario? Why does Susan's fiancé—a weatherman with the emotional depth of a puddle—get more screen time than some actual monsters? And perhaps most puzzling: an alien invasion force capable of interstellar travel is somehow bested by creatures whose collective superpowers include "being big" and "having bug eyes." The movie doesn't so much resolve its logic as steamroll past it, hoping the 3D effects distract you.

**The Pixar Comparison Nobody Asked For, But Here We Are**

This is where "Monsters vs. Aliens" stumbles hardest. Pixar built an empire on marrying spectacle with genuine emotional stakes—think "WALL-E's" wordless heartbreak or "Up's" opening montage that reduced grown adults to sobbing messes. DreamWorks, meanwhile, seems to believe that if you throw enough monster puns and Rick Moranis references at the wall, emotional resonance will simply happen by osmosis.

The film wants us to care about Susan's journey toward self-acceptance and empowerment, but it's so busy cramming in visual gags and government satire that her arc feels like an afterthought squeezed between explosions. Compare this to "Ratatouille," which trusted its audience to sit with quiet moments about passion and identity. "Monsters vs. Aliens" barely lets you exhale before the next set piece.

**What Actually Works**

To be fair, the voice cast is stacked—Hugh Laurie's mad scientist cockroach is delightful, and Seth Rogen's blob character provides genuine laughs. The 3D visuals, especially in theaters, offer legitimate "whoa" moments. And there's something charmingly retro about its B-movie monster movie homages, like it's the animated love child of "Godzilla" and "The Blob" raised on a steady diet of Saturday morning cartoons.

**The Verdict**

"Monsters vs. Aliens" is perfectly serviceable popcorn entertainment—colorful, occasionally funny, and forgotten roughly twelve minutes after the credits roll. It's the animated equivalent of a gas station hot dog: satisfying in the moment, structurally questionable, and not something you'd want to examine too closely.

**Rating: 2.5 out of 4 stars**

*Will delight easily distracted children and adults willing to turn their brains temporarily to mush. Will not delight anyone hoping for the next "Toy Story."*

# Monsters vs. Aliens: A Review Nobody Asked For, But Here We Are

Let's get one thing straight: "Monsters vs. Aliens" wants desperately to be your childhood nostalgia trip and your clever adult wink-fest simultaneously, and like most things that try to please everyone, it ends up as a serviceable but forgettable Wednesday afternoon.

The premise is cute enough—Reese Witherspoon voices Susan, a bride-to-be who gets zapped by a meteor on her wedding day and grows to skyscraper proportions, because apparently that's just what happens to women who dare to have main character energy. She's whisked away to a secret government facility populated by fellow "monsters," including Seth Rogen as B.O.B., a gelatinous blob with no brain (a low bar the film sometimes struggles to clear itself), Hugh Laurie as a mad scientist-cockroach hybrid, and Will Arnett doing his Will Arnett thing as a missing link fish-man. The vocal talent here is genuinely stacked, which makes it all the more frustrating when the script gives them so little to actually chew on.

The sci-fi references come fast and lovingly recycled—there's a healthy dose of "The Blob," "Mothra," "Close Encounters," and "The Fly" DNA splattered across every frame, like the writers raided a film school syllabus and called it worldbuilding. It's affectionate pastiche, sure, but affectionate pastiche isn't the same as having something to say. The alien invasion plot (led by a delightfully campy Rainn Wilson) feels like it's checking boxes on a "How to Make a Kids' Sci-Fi Movie" worksheet rather than building genuine stakes.

Here's the real problem: this film came out the same year as "Coraline," and the comparison is not kind. Where "Coraline" trusted its young audience with genuine dread, stunning handcrafted visuals, and a story that actually meant something about neglect and desire, "Monsters vs. Aliens" trusts its audience with... a lot of screaming and CGI that already looked dated within eighteen months. Coraline had button eyes that haunted your dreams; this film has a giant blue woman who mostly just knocks things over while quipping. One film understood that children can handle complexity and darkness. The other assumed they just wanted things to be loud.

The animation itself is perfectly fine in that early-Dreamworks-3D-gimmick way, clearly engineered for glasses-wearing audiences rather than any lasting artistic vision. It's the cinematic equivalent of cotton candy: entertaining while it's in your mouth, gone the moment you swallow, and you can't quite remember why you wanted it in the first place.

**Final verdict:** A perfectly adequate babysitter of a movie that will not haunt your dreams, expand your mind, or really linger in your memory past the credits—which, ironically, is probably the least "monstrous" thing about it. 2.5 out of 5 giant blue stars.

# Monsters vs. Aliens: A CGI Spectacle That's All Sizzle, No Steak

Let's get one thing straight: I walked into "Monsters vs. Aliens" ready to have a blast. A giant woman! A cockroach-man! Seth Rogen voicing a blob! What's not to love? Turns out, quite a bit, actually.

The film follows Susan Murphy (Reese Witherspoon), a bride-to-be who gets zapped by a meteor on her wedding day and grows to 49 feet tall, because apparently that's just what happens now in DreamWorks movies. She's rebranded "Ginormica" and shipped off to a secret government facility where she meets a ragtag crew of monsters that feels like the Island of Misfit Toys got a Hollywood makeover: B.O.B. (Rogen), a brainless blue gelatin creature; Dr. Cockroach (Hugh Laurie doing his best mad scientist impression, which, let's be honest, is his default setting at this point); The Missing Link (Will Arnett, basically playing Gob Bluth as a fish-man); and Insectosaurus, a giant grub who's essentially this universe's answer to Godzilla, if Godzilla were adorable and mute.

The plot kicks into gear when an alien named Gallaxhar (Rainn Wilson, clearly having the time of his life) invades Earth searching for the same mysterious element that turned Susan into a skyscraper. Cue explosions, government conspiracy jokes, and a genuinely inspired homage to "The Blob" and "Close Encounters" that suggests somewhere in this production, someone really loves classic sci-fi.

Here's the problem: for a movie stuffed with visual gags and a killer voice cast, "Monsters vs. Aliens" plays like it's afraid to commit to being anything beyond serviceable. The jokes land with the frequency of a founding member of a laugh track—present, but oddly mechanical. Stephen Colbert voices the President with the kind of smug delivery that should be hilarious but gets buried under pacing that never quite finds its rhythm. It's the cinematic equivalent of a mixtape where every song is fine, but nothing makes you want to hit repeat.

The 3D effects—and this was peak "everything must be 3D" era, mind you—are genuinely impressive, offering some legitimately cool depth-of-field moments that make the Golden Gate Bridge destruction sequence feel like the money shot it's clearly meant to be. But spectacle can only carry a film so far before you start noticing the screenplay is doing the narrative equivalent of treading water.

Witherspoon brings warmth to Susan's identity crisis—there's a nugget of genuine feminist commentary buried in here about a woman finding her worth outside of marriage—but the film seems almost embarrassed by its own thoughtfulness, constantly retreating to the safety of pratfalls and reaction shots.

Kids will likely enjoy the chaos. Adults might find themselves checking phones during the third act. It's not the disaster its title character could cause if she sat on a city, but it's not the animated classic DreamWorks was clearly hoping for, either.

**Grade: C+** — Imagine "Independence Day" had a baby with "Honey, I Blew Up the Kid," then that baby got its personality from a Saturday morning cartoon. Fun in flashes, forgettable in totality.

# 'Monsters vs. Aliens': A Middling Mashup That Never Quite Escapes Orbit

DreamWorks Animation's 2009 outing "Monsters vs. Aliens" arrives with a game voice cast, eye-popping 3D visuals, and a premise ripe with comedic potential. Unfortunately, what could have been an inspired genre mashup settles for being merely serviceable—entertaining enough for a Saturday matinee, but forgettable by Sunday.

**The Plot Problem**

The story follows Susan Murphy (Reese Witherspoon), who grows to 49 feet, 11 inches after being struck by a meteor on her wedding day, joining a ragtag team of government-quarantined monsters to fight an alien invasion. The setup is charming, but the execution feels like a checklist of beats borrowed from better films. Character motivations shift conveniently whenever the plot requires it, and the emotional arc—Susan's growth (pun intended) into self-actualized confidence—gets undercut by pacing that rushes through character development in favor of action set pieces.

**Physics? What Physics?**

Let's address the elephant—or rather, the 50-foot woman—in the room. The film's relationship with basic physics is casual at best. Susan's mass apparently increases with her height, yet she moves with the agility of someone a fraction of her size, defying the square-cube law that would realistically leave a being her size unable to support her own weight, let alone perform acrobatics. Buildings crumble conveniently around her without the corresponding force one might expect from a woman of her density making contact with concrete. It's animated fantasy, sure, but even cartoon physics usually establish internal consistency—something "Monsters vs. Aliens" never bothers with.

**Reading Too Much Into the Subtext?**

Some critics have pointed to uncomfortable undertones in the film's central metaphor: a woman whose empowerment literally makes her "too big" for society, framed as a problem to be managed by shadowy government forces before she can be useful. The alien invasion subplot, meanwhile, leans on tired tropes of a menacing, technologically superior "other" (voiced with faux-menace by Rainn Wilson) that invites easy, if unexamined, parallels to xenophobic invasion narratives common in genre fiction. Whether intentional commentary or incidental baggage from genre convention, the film doesn't seem interested in exploring these threads with any depth—they're just there, unresolved, beneath the slime and screwball comedy.

**The Verdict**

Visually inventive and occasionally funny, "Monsters vs. Aliens" ultimately feels like a film assembled from spare parts of better movies—part "Ghostbusters," part "Iron Giant," part "Men in Black"—without finding its own distinct identity. B.O.B. (Seth Rogen), the brainless blue blob, provides the film's funniest moments, but comic relief can only carry a film so far when the connective tissue feels this thin.

Still, credit where due: for all its shortcomings, "Monsters vs. Aliens" is "Citizen Kane" compared to that same year's "Space Chimps," a film so tonally confused and visually cheap it makes DreamWorks' effort look like a masterclass in craft by comparison. If nothing else, parents dragging kids to the multiplex this spring should count their blessings that the primates stayed home.

**Rating: 2.5/4 stars**

# "Monsters vs. Aliens": A Groundbreaking Achievement in Mediocrity

Ladies and gentlemen, gather round, because DreamWorks has done it again. They've taken a perfectly reasonable premise—giant monsters fighting aliens—and somehow transformed it into a feature-length toy commercial with delusions of grandeur. Truly, "Monsters vs. Aliens" is the cinematic equivalent of a participation trophy: technically an achievement, but nobody's quite sure why we're celebrating.

## The Cast: A Murderers' Row of Contractual Obligations

Reese Witherspoon voices Susan Murphy, a woman who grows to fifty feet tall on her wedding day, which is either a bold feminist metaphor or the writers running out of ideas after "what if a woman got really big?" Witherspoon brings her signature charm to the role, which is impressive considering she's essentially voicing a Google search for "empowerment."

Seth Rogen plays a gelatinous blob named B.O.B., which stands for absolutely nothing important, much like his character's contribution to the plot. Hugh Laurie shows up as a cockroach scientist, presumably because someone thought, "What if House, but bugs?" And Stephen Colbert voices the President, delivering political satire so toothless it makes a children's dentist look terrifying.

## Animation: Pixels Doing Their Best

The 3D animation is serviceable in the way that a Denny's menu is "serviceable"—technically food, technically motion. DreamWorks clearly poured resources into making things fly toward the camera in ways that scream "THIS WAS DESIGNED FOR 3D GLASSES," rather than, say, character development. The monsters themselves look fine, if you enjoy character designs that seem workshopped by a committee that included "the guy who does Trix cereal boxes."

## Feminist Themes: A Valiant, Confused Effort

Ah yes, the film's stab at feminism—and "stab" is generous, more like a gentle poke with a foam pool noodle. Susan's arc is ostensibly about a woman finding her own identity outside of her fiancé's shadow, which is a lovely idea buried under fifty layers of slime jokes and a robot that shoots lasers.

The film wants desperately to be empowering: Susan literally becomes larger than life! She saves the day! She doesn't need a man! And yet, the movie can't resist making her insecurities the butt of jokes for a solid forty minutes before her "growth." It's feminism by way of a fortune cookie—technically has a message, but you're not sure it was thought through by anyone with actual convictions.

## Final Verdict

"Monsters vs. Aliens" is exactly what it sounds like: a mildly entertaining, forgettable romp that exists primarily to sell Happy Meals and prove that yes, even in animation, you can coast on premise alone. It's not bad, per se—it's just profoundly, aggressively *fine*, like lukewarm tap water served with a side of "we tried."

**Rating: 2.5 Giant Slime Monsters out of 5**
